The largest voluntary biodiversity credit transaction in history happened in October.

CDC Biodiversité sold $1m worth of credits from its Tourbières Tuile Pradeaux site, 13% of everything this market has sold since 2022. A milestone for France Crédits Biodiversité and for the market.

We asked CDC for the buyer's identification and data, but have not yet received any. Apparently nothing can be shared until communication is agreed between them, which will take at least another month.

This opacity makes us question the overall market's relation to data sharing. By value, 63% of all corporate purchases ever made are anonymous. Most developers publish a price and a volume, and stop there. After four years and more than $8m of sales, the market still has no common approach to transparency.

Without buyer data, potential buyers cannot see that their peers are moving on credits, investors cannot size the demand, developers cannot target their outreach, and the people designing national schemes work from isolated cases. Each anonymous transaction removes data that everyone in the market could benefit from.

In our experience, this market moves forward through trust, and transparency is one of the best ways to build it. Even when a buyer prefers to stay anonymous, for reasons we understand, there is a lot of value in sharing its sector, size, country and reason for buying. The commercial sensitivity is much lower, and it is exactly what the market is missing.

This is the main story in this month's Monthly Market Overview, alongside twenty governments launching the Friends of Credits for Nature and Biodiversity at COP17, Indonesia saying it wants its market to be mandatory, ten countries moving up our Countries ladder in one month, Cercarbono launching its Nature Integrity Methodology at COP31, and the IAPB's new way to price a credit against direct investment.

posts.text: NEW BIS RULE – The BIS rule tightens US AI-chip export controls to stop Chinese companies bypassing restrictions by renting computing power from overseas data centres rather than buying chips directly. Released yesterday by the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, it was written by and at the direction of Treasury and the National Security Council. It formally rescinds the earlier, unenforced AI Diffusion Rule.It introduces licensing requirements for advanced chips and servers used by data centres worldwide to provide substantial computing capacity to Chinese and other restricted companies. It also adds chip-export licensing requirements for Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, and tightens customer checks and foundry controls, with certain exemptions for US-headquartered recipients and commercial recommendation systems. The aim is to close the offshore-compute loophole and protect US national security. The likely impact is higher compliance costs and greater uncertainty for chip suppliers and cloud operators, potentially more expensive or restricted access to advanced compute for Chinese AI developers, and delays to affected chip shipments and data-centre projects—not a blanket ban on overseas AI investment. Tighter compute access is also seen as a risk to AI model training and Chinese cloud revenue growth. Licence approvals will be considered case by case.

CE-25A Flew 16 Minutes. The Investment Play Is Not The Plane.

China's CE-25A electric aircraft just did its first crewed flight in Shandong after 19 unmanned tests.

I don't see this as an aviation story. I see it as a convergence story.

Electric aviation only works if 4 stacks mature together:
1. Battery energy density
2. Power management
3. Lightweight materials
4. Predictive maintenance via AI

Those same 4 stacks power EVs, humanoids, and industrial robotics.

So the opportunity is not COMAC. It's the suppliers: battery developers, advanced materials, automation, energy infra.

Risks are real: certification, safety, cost per kWh, range at 400km / 300kmh is still short-haul only.

For Indonesia, an archipelago dependent on air connectivity, the question is practical: which part of this supply chain can we co-build, not just buy?

Where are you placing your bet: batteries, materials, or AI for operational efficiency?

On 3 November, NTT DATA opened its Jakarta 2 Annex, with 12 MW of IT capacity.

The buildings get the headlines. The people who keep them running get less attention. A site that promises uptime all year needs a site head, engineers who know power and cooling, and someone who can manage clients on strict contracts.

Every new operator will look first at the people who have already run a facility like this. That group is small, so it helps to look further.

Two suggestions for companies building or expanding in this sector.

Look at adjacent industries. Power plants, large manufacturing sites and telecom networks also run critical equipment around the clock, and their leaders know what an outage costs.

Hire the site leader before commissioning. That person should help choose the team that will run the site, not inherit one.
